title: Mohnish Pabrai's Session at The University of Nebraska, Omaha on May 3, 2024
summary: On the eve of the 2024 Berkshire meeting, Pabrai floats two half-formed ideas: that there is an 'owner intrinsic value' distinct from standard intrinsic value (Buffett the individual never sold Berkshire even when Berkshire the company issued shares), and that Buffett's rare hits come only every five years because circle of competence grows slowly (See's Candies in 1972 had to precede Coke in 1988). The Q&A covers not talking to management, young investors' edge, memories of Charlie Munger, cloning, the IPSCO and Consol Energy 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bets, no-debt businesses, China, crypto, and parenting.

ideas.idea: Circle the wagons: when you own a business with great economics and prospects, hang on and do not get cute about overvaluation or switching; less activity is more profitable.
ideas.detail: He revisits the 'circling the wagons' concept from his 2023 talk and admits it skims over intrinsic value, which remains the bedrock; every business has a finite value.

ideas.idea: There are two intrinsic values: the standard discounted-cash-flow value and an 'owner intrinsic value' that looks much further out and includes intangibles like control.
ideas.detail: In 1990 Berkshire traded at ~$4,000 a share (~$6 billion market cap) and a 2x-book shorthand gave maybe $6,000-8,000, but discounting the actual 1990-2024 cash flows gives far more than $10,000-20,000. Berkshire the company issued shares for Dexter and Burlington Northern and buys back below 1.2x tangible book, yet Buffett the individual has never bought or sold a share in almost 60 years; Warren the individual grasped Berkshire's value better than Berkshire the company did.

ideas.idea: Book value is an inadequate measure of Berkshire; Buffett and Munger's own range is likely under 2x book, which is probably conservative.
ideas.detail: They paid over 3x book for See's, and replacing Burlington Northern would cost $700-800 billion or more than a trillion, exceeding Berkshire's market cap, yet its earnings power does not match that. Berkshire trades at about 1.5x book today.

ideas.idea: He has refused every offer to sell a stake in the general partner of Pabrai Investment Funds because he cannot bound its intrinsic value and selling would put a clock on the business.
ideas.detail: Over 25 years the GP's pre-tax margin has been about 88% of fees, 'better than Apple'; the upper end of its value range could be spectacular, and any buyer would eventually want to monetize.

ideas.idea: You only need to get rich once and you only need to be right once; a large error rate is normal even for Buffett.
ideas.detail: Of 100 stock investments 90-plus percent might fail and a few can still make the portfolio great. The FT reported Buffett bought and sold 65 stocks with an average holding period just over four years, and Todd and Ted's average was under three years.

ideas.idea: Think about a business the way its owner would (Howard Schultz for Starbucks, Ken Langone for Home Depot) so you can look past speed bumps and hold for decades.
ideas.detail: Starbucks was 'taken out back and shot' in the last few days and it is hard to tell in real time if it is a speed bump or secular. Ken Langone held Home Depot for four decades with no financial analysis, just 'I bet on people' and loyalty, and got a 40-bagger in Eli Lilly on the side through inactivity.

ideas.idea: Buffett's great hits come only about once every five years because circle of competence grows very slowly; the See's Candies purchase in 1972 made the Coke investment in 1988 possible.
ideas.detail: Of maybe 300-600 decisions in 58 years only about 12 (2-3%) created Berkshire. Without See's there would be no Coke and probably no Apple, since all were bets on brands. For the rest of us it may be one great idea every 25 years.

ideas.idea: See's taught Buffett the power of pricing: he raised prices 10-12% a year every December 26th against 3-4% inflation and volumes still rose 2%, but See's could never expand beyond California.
ideas.detail: Berkshire paid $25 million for See's and has collected more than $2 billion in dividends. Repeated store openings in Chicago and New York lost money; Coke by contrast had no trouble travelling (only Cuba and North Korea lack it), so Coke was a 'home run to the power of a home run' and Berkshire put a quarter of book value into it.

ideas.idea: Access to management is often a negative; insiders are salespeople who lead you astray, so individual investors without access actually have an advantage.
ideas.detail: Buffett and Munger never contacted Coke management; they read about 70 years of annual reports and noticed unit volumes never fell, not in the Depression, the World Wars, Korea or 1970s stagflation. Pabrai says he has been led astray by many managers and it is better not to talk to them.

ideas.idea: Young investors have an edge because change arrives on college campuses first; list every dollar you spend and research the public companies behind it.
ideas.detail: College students were first to drop landlines, cut the cable cord and use Facebook; many restaurant chains start in college towns. Being a consumer gives you non-quantitative data that is a big edge.

ideas.idea: To start a fund, first build an auditable track record with your own money for 5-15 years, then raise from friends, family and fools.
ideas.detail: Only after you have a few hits that worked really well should you convince others you are the one to manage their money.

ideas.idea: He ignored a Clemson professor's advice to switch from engineering to business in 1984-85 and made the switch about 15 years later than he should have.
ideas.detail: He had a 106% average in an investing class; a Disney case study showed the stock at 6-7x earnings with real estate worth more than the market cap. He first heard of Buffett 8-9 years later.

ideas.idea: Most of what he learned from Charlie Munger came from observing how he lived, not from what he said or wrote: he never complained, ate whatever was put in front of him, and 'tried to be useful'.
ideas.detail: His last dinner with Charlie was exactly a month before he died; nearly blind and in pain, Charlie said any morning without a new pain is a great day. Peanut brittle was rationed twice a month and Charlie never asked for more. Charlie helped Berkshire, Costco and Mohnish with no economic interest.

ideas.idea: Cloning is extremely powerful: nothing he knows he came up with himself, and the world is full of great models with no clones, like Chipotle.
ideas.detail: Jim Sinegal said everything he knew came from Sol Price, and Costco went on to buy Price Club. Pabrai wrote about Chipotle in The Dhandho Investor in 2006-07 but never invested; Bill Ackman made the money, and even today nobody has cloned Chipotle (Baja Fresh was terrible).

ideas.idea: 'Heads I win, tails I don't lose much' is the cornerstone of investing; focus on eliminating the downside and the upside takes care of itself.
ideas.detail: Buffett as a child walked with knees bent so he would never fall; he still calls Dexter Shoe a $10-15 billion mistake because 2% of Berkshire's shares went to zero.

ideas.idea: IPSCO in 2004 was the classic downside-protected bet: $45 stock with $15 cash and contracted earnings of $15 a share for two years, so the plant and inventory came free.
ideas.detail: He had no idea of long-term intrinsic value; he just wanted to own it two years and see what Mr. Market did. It doubled in 15 months, then a Swedish company bid $160 and he sold in five seconds.

ideas.idea: Consol Energy in 2023 was 'another IPSCO': a market cap under $2 billion with about $600 million of next-year cash flow already locked in by forward coal sales, a 150-year record of never losing money, and all cash going to buybacks.
ideas.detail: The idea came from a tweet comparing David Einhorn's Consol bet to his IPSCO bet. Consol is the lowest-cost producer of some of the highest-quality thermal coal, so unlike IPSCO it is unlikely to have a losing year; the Baltimore bridge collapse has hurt shipping for a couple of months. It led him on to metallurgical coal.

ideas.idea: A stock that never reaches intrinsic value is a huge positive, not a negative, because the company can buy back shares cheaply and you collect the cash flows.
ideas.detail: He disagrees with Einhorn, who complains that over-indexing leaves companies undervalued for extended periods. He would love Consol's price to stay low for a very long time; 'Go Nvidia', let all the money go to the Fab Four. The market is ultimately a weighing machine.

ideas.idea: All knowledge is cumulative: most investors could not buy Consol because coal is a four-letter word and they lacked the IPSCO framework.
ideas.detail: His reason for buying Consol differed from Einhorn's even though he took the idea from him; everything must be viewed through Munger's lens of opportunity cost, and beauty is in the eye of the beholder.

ideas.idea: He focuses on the micro and always starts with the business; macro is beyond his 'little brain'.
ideas.detail: He does not start with the pandemic, US-China tension or the Ukraine war and ask how to make money from them; understanding a single business is complicated enough.

ideas.idea: The best businesses run with zero debt; he is not a proponent of borrowing to buy back shares, and Berkshire's cash overload is the gold standard.
ideas.detail: Buffett and Munger said modest leverage would have improved results but never used it because businesses are fragile and must withstand heavy storms. A hallmark of a great business is high ROE with no leverage; Starbucks and McDonald's borrowing into negative equity is 'not good'.

ideas.idea: Most of China is outside his circle of competence; he should never have sold Moutai, and Alibaba and Tencent did not work for him.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He no longer holds Alibaba or Tencent and only looks at Chinese names to the extent they fall within what he can understand.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs do not take risks; they do everything possible to minimize risk, and you should too.
ideas.detail: At 24 he took $25,000 from his 401(k) and signed up for $70,000 of credit card lines to start his first business, having researched that bankruptcy law would wipe out the debt if it failed; the downside was limited and the upside asymmetric.

ideas.idea: Picking a good investment manager is harder than picking a good investment; default to an index fund unless 'seven moons align'.
ideas.detail: Look for Peter Kaufman's five aces: alignment of interest, track record and how it was built, ethos, character, and fishing where the fish are. Being indexed forever would not be a tragedy.

ideas.idea: Crypto is outside his circle of competence and, echoing Munger, 'rat poison'; a blow-up would not surprise him.
ideas.detail: Blockchain has positives but the crypto world attracts certain kinds of characters; it is an easy pass. Similarly, AI can help narrow the universe but he is skeptical it can replicate a Buffett or Munger template.
